SIP vs Lumpsum: Which Is Better for You?

Both methods put money into the same funds. What differs is timing: a lumpsum is invested all at once, a SIP spreads it out. Here is how each behaves in rising and falling markets, and how to choose.

3 min readUpdated 20 October 2026

The short answer

If you earn a salary and invest from income, a SIP (systematic investment plan) is usually the natural choice: you invest as the money arrives. If you already have a large amount (a bonus, maturity proceeds, an inheritance), the question is whether to invest it at once or spread it out. Investing at once has tended to win when markets rise steadily; spreading it out reduces the regret and risk of investing just before a fall. Neither is guaranteed to give the higher return.

How each method works

  • Lumpsum: you invest the whole amount on one day and buy units at that day's NAV (net asset value). All your money is exposed to the market from day one.
  • SIP: you invest a fixed amount every month (or week). Each instalment buys units at that date's NAV, so you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
  • Both can be used with the same mutual fund, the same expense ratio and the same tax rules. The only difference is when your money enters the market.

Example 1: a falling and recovering market

You have ₹60,000. Option A invests it all in month 1. Option B invests ₹10,000 a month for six months. The NAV falls from ₹100 to ₹60 and then recovers to ₹120.

MonthNAV (₹)SIP units bought (₹10,000 each)

The SIP bought 700 units at an average cost of about ₹85.71 (₹60,000 ÷ 700), worth ₹84,000 at the final NAV of ₹120. The lumpsum bought 600 units at ₹100, worth ₹72,000. Here the SIP wins by ₹12,000, because it kept buying cheaply during the fall. This is rupee cost averaging.

Example 2: a steadily rising market

Same ₹60,000, but the NAV rises every month: ₹100, 105, 110, 115, 120 and 125.

MethodUnitsValue at NAV ₹125
Lumpsum in month 1600.00₹75,000
SIP of ₹10,000 a month536.44₹67,055

In a rising market the lumpsum wins by about ₹7,945, because all of the money was invested at the lowest price. The SIP kept buying at higher prices. Over long periods markets have risen more often than they have fallen, which is why investing a lumpsum early has often done better, but no one knows in advance which kind of period lies ahead.

What rupee cost averaging does and does not do

  • It lowers your average cost compared with the average NAV over the period, because a fixed amount buys more units when prices are low.
  • It reduces the risk of putting everything in at a market peak.
  • It does not guarantee a profit or protect against a loss if prices stay low.
  • It does not beat a lumpsum in a market that rises steadily from the start.

A middle path for large amounts: STP

With a systematic transfer plan (STP), you put the lumpsum into a low-risk fund (such as a liquid fund) and transfer a fixed amount each month into an equity fund, typically over 6 to 12 months. Your money earns something while it waits and still enters equity gradually. Check the exit load and the tax on each transfer, because every transfer is a redemption from the first fund.

How to decide

  • Investing from monthly income: use a SIP. It builds the habit and needs no market timing.
  • Large amount and a long horizon (10 years or more): investing it at once or over a few months both work; choose the one you will stick with if the market falls right after.
  • Large amount and you would panic at a sudden 20% fall: spread it over 6 to 12 months with an STP.
  • Money needed within 3 years: neither belongs in equity funds; consider debt funds or deposits.
  • Always keep an emergency fund of 3 to 6 months of expenses before investing in equity.

Common questions

Is SIP safer than lumpsum?

A SIP spreads your entry over time, which reduces timing risk, but the investment itself carries the same market risk. If the fund falls and stays down, both methods lose money.

Can I do both SIP and lumpsum in the same fund?

Yes. Many investors run a monthly SIP and add lumpsums when they receive a bonus or other extra money.

Is tax different for SIP and lumpsum?

The tax rules are the same, but each SIP instalment is a separate purchase with its own holding period. When you redeem, units are sold first-in, first-out, so the most recent instalments may count as short-term.

Should I stop my SIP when the market falls?

Usually not. Falls are when a SIP buys the most units at low prices, which is the main benefit of rupee cost averaging. Stop only if your goals or finances have changed.
